title.en: Explain the formation of the depletion region
Describe the barrier potential and its values
State the effect of bias on the depletion width

say.en: Join p-type and n-type silicon in one crystal and something remarkable happens at the boundary: a thin layer with no free carriers and a built-in voltage appears. In this lesson: Explain the formation of the depletion region.
Describe the barrier potential and its values.
State the effect of bias on the depletion width.

body.en: At the junction, holes diffuse from p to n and electrons from n to p, where they recombine. They leave behind fixed negative acceptor ions on the p-side and fixed positive donor ions on the n-side. This thin layer, empty of free carriers, is the *depletion region* (space-charge region). Its ions set up an electric field from n to p that opposes further diffusion.

points.en: *Diffusion* of majority carriers across the junction
*Depletion region*: immobile ions, no free carriers

narration.en: Majority carriers diffuse across the junction and recombine, leaving fixed ions. This carrier-free layer is the depletion region, and its field from n to p stops further diffusion.
narration.kn: ಬಹುಸಂಖ್ಯಾತ ವಾಹಕಗಳು ಸಂಧಿಯನ್ನು ದಾಟಿ ಪುನರ್ಸಂಯೋಜನೆಗೊಂಡು ಸ್ಥಿರ ಅಯಾನುಗಳನ್ನು ಬಿಡುತ್ತವೆ. ವಾಹಕರಹಿತ ಈ ಪದರವೇ ಸವಕಳಿ ಪ್ರದೇಶ; ಅದರ n ನಿಂದ p ಕಡೆಗಿನ ಕ್ಷೇತ್ರ ಮುಂದಿನ ವಿಸರಣವನ್ನು ತಡೆಯುತ್ತದೆ.

say.en: Depletion region: immobile ions, no free carriers.
Field from n-side to p-side.
Join a p-type piece and an n-type piece. The p-side has many holes; the n-side has many free electrons.
Carriers diffuse across and recombine. Near the junction only fixed ions are left: negative on the p-side, positive on the n-side. This is the depletion region.
The ions set up a field from the n-side to the p-side. It stops further diffusion.
The potential rises across the region by the barrier potential: about 0.7 volt for silicon and 0.3 volt for germanium.

body.en: The field corresponds to a potential difference across the depletion region called the *barrier potential* V₀: about 0.7 V for silicon and 0.3 V for germanium at room temperature. In equilibrium the diffusion current is balanced by an equal and opposite drift current of minority carriers, so no net current flows. V₀ increases with doping: $V_0 = V_T\ln(N_A N_D/n_i^2)$. Forward bias narrows the depletion region; reverse bias widens it.

points.en: Si: V₀ ≈ 0.7 V; Ge: V₀ ≈ 0.3 V
Forward bias narrows, reverse bias widens the region

problem.en: A silicon junction has N_A = 10¹⁷ cm⁻³, N_D = 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ and nᵢ = 1.5 × 10¹⁰ cm⁻³. Find the barrier potential at 300 K (V_T = 25.85 mV).

narration.en: Let us solve this together. A silicon junction has N_A = 10¹⁷ cm⁻³, N_D = 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ and nᵢ = 1.5 × 10¹⁰ cm⁻³. Find the barrier potential at 300 K (V_T = 25.85 mV).

say.en: Let us solve this together. A silicon junction has N A equals 10 to the power 17 centimetres to the power minus 3, N D equals 10 to the power 16 centimetres to the power minus 3 and n i equals 1.5 times 10 to the power 10 centimetres to the power minus 3. Find the barrier potential at 300 kelvin V T equals 25.85 mV.
N A N D divided by n i squared equals 10 to the power 33 / (2.25 times 10 to the power 20) equals 4.44 times 10 to the power 12.
ln(4.44 times 10 to the power 12) is approximately 29.12.
V 0 equals 0.02585 times 29.12 is approximately 0.753 volts.
So the answer is V 0 is approximately 0.75 volts.

The n-side of the depletion region has positive donor ions and the p-side has negative acceptor ions, so the field points from n to p.
It opposes further diffusion of majority carriers.
